function.mechanism: Inhibits growth of spoilage microorganisms (especially yeasts and moulds) as a paraben antimicrobial preservative.
common_food_categories: processed foods where preservative use is permitted

adi.basis: EFSA (2004) full group ADI 0-10 for the sum of methyl and ethyl p-hydroxybenzoate esters and sodium salts; propyl excluded.

efsa.key_finding: EFSA retained a group ADI for methyl/ethyl parabens and concluded propyl paraben should not be included due to reproductive findings and lack of clear NOAEL.

adi.basis: JECFA group ADI 0-10 mg/kg bw as the sum of ethyl, methyl, and propyl esters of p-hydroxybenzoic acid.

concerns.summary: Parabens show weak in-vitro estrogenic activity; EFSA reported no in-vivo uterotrophic activity for methyl paraben in reviewed classical assays, leaving mechanistic concern but limited in-vivo confirmation for E218.

A recent mouse study reported metabolic disorder and liver damage with a gut-microbiome-linked mechanism under experimental exposure conditions, with uncertain direct translation to typical dietary human exposure.
Recent aquatic and rodent models report reproductive or developmental perturbations under laboratory exposures, but human epidemiologic evidence remains limited and mixed.

no_concern_confirmed: EFSA 2004 reported no developmental toxicity for methyl paraben in reviewed mouse, rat, hamster, and rabbit studies up to highest tested doses.
EFSA 2004 considered 1000 mg/kg bw/day a NOAEL for methyl paraben in juvenile-rat male reproductive endpoint studies reviewed by the panel.

populations: children with higher intake per body weight
high consumers with cumulative paraben exposure from multiple food categories
adi_exceedance.notes: EFSA (2004) indicated then-available conservative intake estimates were below ADI but also noted exposure characterization gaps; recent scoping review literature indicates possible cumulative exceedance scenarios.

risk_assessment.rationale: Regulatory approval and ADI frameworks in EU/US/JECFA support continued permitted use, but mechanistic/endocrine and experimental toxicology signals plus exposure uncertainty argue against a lower-risk classification.
key_factors: EFSA group ADI exists for methyl/ethyl parabens (0-10 mg/kg bw/day)
FDA lists methylparaben as GRAS in 21 CFR 184.1490 with GMP maximum 0.1% in food
No IARC carcinogenic classification identified for methylparaben
Recent studies suggest plausible mechanistic concerns and cumulative exposure uncertainty
